title: AI Designing Chips Is Real; Verification Is Still the Number One Bottleneck
dek: AI can already write RTL on its own, but the real chokepoint in the whole chip pipeline is verification: it eats more than half of development time, and AI still cannot answer "what should be tested." OpenAI's twenty-person team can shorten the front end, but the back end still has to be left to humans.
why: The author uses what he saw firsthand and the words of frontline engineers to pull "AI builds chips" out of clickbait: which parts are prototypes, which can go into production, and where the moat actually is.
who: Semiconductor investors trying to judge whether "AI designs chips" is a real inflection point or fundraising talk, chip company decision-makers, and engineers watching AI deployment.
skip: The EDA terminology primer at the start (minute 1); anyone who knows the chip design flow can skip it.

points.h: K3 has only a front end, no back end
points.body: The source material for "AI tapes out in 48 hours" is a small inference accelerator Kimi announced called Nano KPU: 238,000 parameters, about 1.46 million standard cells, 0.277MB SRAM, claimed to close timing at 100 MHz within 4 square millimeters with decode throughput of 8,700 tokens/s. But the host looked closely: this batch of RTL only did functional verification, with no cell placement, routing, physical verification or sign-off; the so-called "timing closure" relies on estimates, 100 MHz is not impressive in a 45nm open-source library where a human using the same library can hit 20-450 MHz, and commercial processes can reach 1-3 GHz. K3's goal was not to build a good chip, but to prove an agent can autonomously reach functional completeness.

points.h: AI writing RTL is not news at all
points.body: Many people think AI writing chips only started with K3, but back in 2020 someone at NYU used GPT-2 to generate beginner-level RTL, with reports citing 94.8% accuracy; the now-defunct eFabless ran an AI design contest, and a design Will Salcedo generated with GPT-4 actually went to tapeout, one of the earliest LLM-designed tapeouts the host knows of. "AI writes RTL" is not itself the innovation; what actually changed is that an agent can run unattended from start to functional completeness — the autonomy of the flow has been forged.

points.h: The agent's future is being wrapped around the toolchain
points.body: While fully autonomous design is still nowhere in sight, the real product form is wrapping an LLM around the EDA toolchain: the LLM directs deterministic EDA tools through interfaces like MCP and APIs, just as Claude Code lets a model call computer tools. The long-term goal of Synopsys, Cadence and Siemens is to open up their own stacks and hand data feedback and control to agents that can run for hours or overnight. Siemens played a demo at Semicon Taiwan: having an agent drop hundreds of standard cells one by one into a simulator to measure load, speed and power for later designs to look up. Redoing this tedious work for every process node change is exactly the kind of thing to hand to AI before leaving the office.

points.h: Even the best results cannot do without a human in the loop
points.body: The post by former xAI engineer Christina Lee is, in the host's eyes, the most convincing breakdown. Her meta-harness has an inner and an outer layer: the inner layer has the model call EDA tools to write RTL, synthesize, place and route, and verify; the outer layer has the model review what was right and wrong in the previous round, propose improvements and run again. The first stage only did a MAC multiply-accumulate array, iterating over multiple rounds to 900 MHz to 1 GHz; the second stage connected the MAC to SRAM and other modules, and complexity rose immediately. Note that the human always holds the steering wheel: the so-called goal strings are very likely provided as reference by the outer model, but the filtering and final confirmation power is in human hands. AI is not the boss, it is the co-pilot.

points.h: What is truly scary about Jalapeno is the 20-person team
points.body: OpenAI's Jalapeno demo had many people fixating on "only 9 months from RTL to tapeout." The host reminds us: Synopsys had previously said on an unrelated occasion that using their tools without AI also takes about 9 to 12 months; the chip itself is not complex, and the starting point is unclear — the architecture concept only began in October 2024. What really stands out is the team size: only 20 to 30 people stood up when the talk ended. And this group's token consumption ranked at the top of OpenAI's internal leaderboard year-round, with RTL still being changed the day before freeze. If a team this small can build it, future chip roles will need an order of magnitude fewer people, which may be exactly why they did not emphasize it in the slides.

points.h: Verification is the real chokepoint in AI chip design
points.body: The whole industry talks up the front-end RTL while glossing over the back end: OpenAI's launch slides dwell a lot on spec and RTL, and the host guesses the back end was probably handled by partner Broadcom, thanked in a single line on slide 34; Lee also handed the back end to Yosys/OpenLane. The mechanistic asymmetry is this: PPA (power/performance/area) optimization is a closed loop — generate, verify, measure PPA — and AI has a clear reward signal; verification is not, because a test passing or failing does not tell AI how far it is from full coverage, and "what should be tested" still can only come from humans. A chip bug cannot be changed once taped out, so seeing a defect the first time you lay eyes on the TSMC silicon is the most crushing thing. This explains why verification can eat 50 to 70% of development time, and echoes Shibo Chen's line that "AI does the design, humans do the verification" is what makes people comfortable.

points.h: The front-end wrapper's biggest enemy is OpenAI
points.body: A large number of startups have sprung up in Silicon Valley wrapping frontier models with proprietary knowledge to write RTL. The risk the host sees is this: Anthropic and OpenAI themselves both own the models and are building chips, and the moment they decide to open up the models used for chips, the front-end wrapper's differentiation is gone. So he prefers to look at teams moving toward the back end and verification, where end-to-end is the only moat. How fast is this field moving? Just as he was writing, Architect Labs announced that the Redwood chip was produced and verified entirely by AI, with the spec written only by two architects; even TSMC's 3D IC talk used "agentic AI." The host himself worries his judgment will be overturned by new news in a week or two.

The confidential process parameter package maintained jointly by foundries and EDA vendors, tightly protected under NDA.
The three major metrics for judging chip design quality, directly usable for closed-loop optimization.

The problems are going to get ironed out because customers demand this and we're getting a situation where the AI and domain experts are putting their heads together to solve problems. The future is here, old man.
